summary: A 1970 note describing a prototype implementation of the Network Control Program (NCP), the host software handling network communication. It was written by members of the UCLA group.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 55 gives a prose example of a possible Network Control Program implementation. It explains how the NCP might manage connections, buffers, and messages, but says the design is not a required model.

what is the ncp prototype in rfc 55
what states did the early ncp use
subtitle: A prose example of how a Network Control Program could be organized.

tldr.problem: The formal NCP protocol did not show how an implementation might organize its programs, tables, and connection handling.
tldr.mechanism: The authors describe system calls, component programs, tables, queues, connection procedures, flow control, and a ten-state model.
tldr.outcome: The RFC explicitly says this is an example, not a model, and that only the rules in RFC 54 must be followed.

today: RFC 55 is listed with status Unknown and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text says it is an example, not a model or specification.

sections.title: Why Describe a Prototype
sections.content:
The authors tried to write an NCP prototype in an Algol-like language but abandoned the effort when the code became unreadable. They wrote a prose description to show how an NCP might be implemented and to help uncover issues in applying the formal specification to existing systems.

The RFC states that nothing in the document is required for implementation. It identifies RFC 54 as the source of the rigid rules an NCP must follow.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors explain one possible implementation to make design issues easier to discuss. They state that this example is not a requirement.

sections.title: Programs and Tables
sections.content:
The proposed NCP has five component programs: input and output handlers, an input interpreter, an output scheduler, and a system-call interpreter. The output scheduler prioritizes Host-to-IMP messages, control messages, and regular messages in that order.

The design uses tables for connection attributes, input and output links, ports, control-command queues, output requests, live hosts, and link assignments. A rendezvous-table entry includes local and foreign sockets, link, connection and flow state, and queues.
sections.plainLanguage: The example splits NCP work among handlers, interpreters, and a scheduler. Tables hold information about sockets, connections, queued messages, and links.

sections.title: Opening and Flow Control
sections.content:
Opening a connection requires an exchange of RFCs, a generic term in this document for RTS and STR messages. Pending calls are queued because messages can arrive before a process issues LISTEN.

Data cannot flow until the connection is open and buffer space has been allocated. The receiver sends ALL messages to grant additional buffer space; the sender reduces its available amount as it transmits data.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides exchange connection requests before data flows. The receiver grants buffer space, and the sender must stay within that amount.

sections.title: Connection States and Closing
sections.content:
The RFC describes a socket state machine with ten states, including CLOSED, LISTENING, RFC-SENT, OPEN, DATA-WAIT, and RFNM-WAIT. Events and local calls move sockets among states.

Closing requires an exchange of CLS commands. A sending side may need to wait for its data buffer to empty and for an RFNM before sending CLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The example tracks each socket through states such as waiting, open, and closing. A sender may have to finish queued data before the connection closes.

references.text: NWG/RFC 54, the protocol rules an NCP must follow.
Kraley, M. and J. Newkirk, "Thoughts and Reflections on NWG/RFC #54", RFC 57, June 1970.
